items.headline: Lyra Systems signs Pentagon CRADA to fast‑track tech to orbit
items.title: Exclusive: Lyra Systems Emerges from Stealth to Solve the Valley of Death
items.scifi_hook: A stealth startup gets a five‑year deal to shepherd new gadgets onto space missions.
items.eli5: Lyra will use AI software to help novel hardware get flight tests with the Air Force.
items.why: It could speed defense innovation and reduce costly development gaps.
items.text: CA-based startup Lyra Systems emerged from stealth on Tuesday, announcing an agreement with the Pentagon aimed at helping early-stage technologies traverse unscathed across the Valley of Death. Under the five-year Cooperative Research and Development Agreement (CRADA) with AFRL, Lyra Systems will aim to use its AI-enabled mission-integration software to help new tech get demo opportunities in orbit faster. The agreement aims to create “a repeatable integration pathway for nontraditional vendors to gain flight heritage,” according to SpaceWERX Senior Engineer Marcus Bracey. The problem: As an industry term, the Valley of Death describes the final resting place for promising technologies that never progressed to demonstration missions or commercial sales. Traditionally, tech development has stalled out mainly due to lack of funding opportunities—but Lyra founder and CEO Tanmayi Sai says the money isn’t the problem anymore. “Budgets and private capital have both more than doubled in defense, and the number of companies that can convert either into a flown mission has barely moved,” she said. “What is missing is the integration work between a qualified component and an operational mission. items.headline: Vale base metals unit targets $5 billion profit by 2026
items.title: Vale Base Metals to triple earnings to $5B for 2026, CEO says
items.scifi_hook: Brazil’s mining giant bets on cheaper copper projects to triple earnings.
items.eli5: Vale plans to boost copper output and cut costs to raise profit threefold.
items.why: Helps secure critical mineral supply amid global demand.
items.text: Vale’s (NYSE: VALE) base metals unit aims to triple pre-tax profit to $5 billion this year, up from about $1.3 billion in 2024, when the business also consumed around $2 billion in cash, CEO Shaun Usmar says. The push reflects sweeping cost reductions, an overhaul of operating accountability after years of missed production targets and about $10 billion in capital project overruns over 18 years, as well as stronger copper prices. Vale’s third-quarter results show its average realized copper price rose 56% year over year to $15,314 per tonne, outpacing a 44% increase in the benchmark London Metal Exchange price. Usmar is now betting that redesigned projects and brownfield expansions near existing infrastructure can deliver growth at substantially lower costs and higher returns. “We aren’t just a turnaround story; we’re also a growth story,” Usmar said Monday at the Canadian Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Petroleum’s (CIM) Capital Projects Symposium in Toronto. The strategy comes as Western governments race to secure critical minerals supplies and reduce their dependence on China, which Usmar says has built a formidable lead through decades of investment in mineral resources and processing capacity. Against that backdrop, VBM is seeking to capitalize on its established mining and processing infrastructure in Canada and its extensive copper holdings in Brazil to expand production faster and at lower cost than developing entirely new operations. items.headline: Cobalt phosphide catalyst stays stable while splitting water for hydrogen
items.title: A catalyst that protects itself while producing hydrogen
items.scifi_hook: A self‑protecting catalyst keeps making hydrogen without degrading, like a robot that never wears out.
items.eli5: Cobalt phosphide works like a durable metal that splits water into hydrogen even in harsh conditions.
items.why: It could lower the cost and boost the reliability of clean hydrogen production.
items.text: Cobalt phosphide (CoP) is a promising alternative to platinum for producing hydrogen from water. However, scientists have struggled to explain why it performs so well. Computer models have suggested that CoP should become unstable under the conditions used to produce hydrogen, yet experiments show that it remains active and durable in acidic, neutral and alkaline environments.

items.headline: Pakistani astronaut to fly on China’s Shenzhou‑24 mission
items.title: China and Pakistan are set to make history in space cooperation
items.scifi_hook: For the first time a foreign astronaut will ride a Chinese crewed spacecraft to the Tiangong station.
items.eli5: China will send a Pakistani space‑flight specialist to join its crew on a mission to the Chinese space station.
items.why: It marks a historic step in international space cooperation and deepens China‑Pakistan ties.
items.text: China has confirmed that a Pakistani astronaut will join the Shenzhou-24 crewed mission as a payload specialist, marking the first time a foreign astronaut will participate in a joint flight mission under China's crewed space program and visit the Chinese space station. In response to a question at Monday's Foreign Ministry press briefing, Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said the mission would be another major milestone in China-Pakistan cooperation, coinciding with the 75th anniversary of diplomatic ties between the two countries.
